4625:     are strictly sequential: one rig, one hole, one dig at a time.  So the
4626:     programme spans `T + (W − 1) × cadence` of calendar, and the articles that
4627:     are bought ONCE at the start and amortised across all of it, the bus NRE,
4628:     the autonomy NRE, and the rig itself, are being carried for far longer
4629:     than one mission duration before the missions they paid for sell anything.
4630: 
4631:     Note which lines this is and is not.  A per-mission article (the launch,
4632:     the capsule, the propellant, the plant, the electric stage) is bought for
4633:     its own campaign, and that campaign's costs AND its revenue both sit at the
4634:     same point in the programme, shift a whole cash flow and its cost/revenue
4635:     ratio does not move.  Only the amortised lines are stretched, because only
4636:     they are paid at t = 0 for a mission that sells at t = w × cadence.
4637: 
4638:     ── The arithmetic ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4639: 
4640:     Campaign w (w = 0 … W−1) sells at `T + w × cadence`, so its share of an
4641:     article bought at t = 0 compounds by `(1+W)^(T + w·cadence)`.  Factor out
4642:     the `(1+W)^T` the caller already applies and average over the programme:
4643: 
4644:         cost   = mean of y^w  for w = 0 … W−1        y = (1 + wacc)^cadence
4645:                = (y^W − 1) / ((y − 1) · W)

974:     ── The window ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
975: 
976:     A programme of F ships repeating every `cadence_yr` puts a delivery on the
977:     market every `cadence / F` years, so in steady state one delivery may sell
978:     `cap x cadence / F`.  Note that is the same constraint as a RATE test, seen
979:     from the other side:
980: 
981:         kg <= cap x cadence / F     <=>     kg x F / cadence <= cap
982: 
983:     The FIRST delivery is different, and it is the one exception this function
984:     makes.  Nothing has arrived yet, so the destination has been importing from
985:     Earth for the whole outbound-and-back trip: `duration_yr`, which is longer
986:     than the cadence, because the cadence is only the dig (or the window),
987:     while the duration is the whole mission.  Over a programme of N deliveries
988:     the market therefore accumulates for
989: 
990:         duration + (N - 1) x cadence / F
991: 
992:     years in total, and this returns the per-delivery average of that.  At
993:     N = 1 it is exactly `cap x duration`; as N grows it converges on the steady
994:     state `cap x cadence / F`.
995: 
996:     ⚠️  IT IS AVERAGED RATHER THAN BRANCHED, deliberately.  Giving delivery one
997:     the long window and every later delivery the short one is the same model,
998:     but as a step it puts a discontinuity between N = 1 and N = 2 that hands
999:     N = 1 a structural advantage no economics produced -- and the ladder would
1000:     then collapse onto N = 1 for a reason that is a rule, not a result.  The
1001:     average is continuous in N and gives the identical answer at both ends.

1026: def _delivery_window_yr(
1027:     n_missions: int, fleet: int, duration_yr: float, cadence_yr: float,
1028: ) -> float:
1029:     """Years of market accumulation behind ONE delivery of a programme.
1030: 
1031:     The single statement of the window algebra `capacity_allowance_kg`
1032:     documents.  Split out because the ladder needs the window ONCE per rung and
1033:     then multiplies it by each commodity's own ceiling; calling the per-
1034:     commodity function would re-derive the same five float operations for every
1035:     phase in the haul, ~60 of them per rung and ~40 rungs per candidate.
1036: 
1037:     Two readers, one derivation.  Writing the expression out again at the call
1038:     site is exactly the "two copies of one algebra drifting apart" hazard the
1039:     mass ledger warns about.
1040:     """
1041:     n      = max(1, int(n_missions))
1042:     f      = max(1, int(fleet))
1043:     first  = max(0.0, float(duration_yr))
1044:     steady = max(0.0, float(cadence_yr)) / f
1045:     return (first + (n - 1) * steady) / n

Even the goal is roughly one flagship RTG a year for the entire world, so any programme flying more than a couple of these does not have a cost problem, it has an allocation problem.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"Eclipse / night-side dark fraction","unit":"fraction of the time a surface rig sees no sun","value":0.5,"range_low":0.35,"range_high":0.55,"notes":"v1.11.0.  A rig anchored to a rotating body stands on a surface that is lit half the time, by geometry — the same 0.50 STORAGE_REFERENCE has carried since v1.9.0, moved here so Module 4 can actually read it.  Ranges below 0.5 for a high-latitude or near-polar emplacement on a body with obliquity, above it for an equatorial site with local horizon shadowing.
This is a SIZING factor, not a specific mass, and that is why no W/kg figure can absorb it: to deliver P continuously through a dark fraction f you must INSTALL P·[(1−f) + f/η_rt]/(1−f) of generating capacity, because the sunlit hours have to run the load and recharge the store as well.  At f = 0.50 and η_rt = 0.90 that is 2.11×.
The alternative architecture is to mine at half duty cycle and take twice the stay time instead; Module 4 sizes the storage rather than halving the duty, which is the choice that leaves mission duration comparable across bodies.
Does NOT apply to a radioisotope source — an RTG's output is flat — and does not apply to the electric-propulsion array, which is in interplanetary cruise and in permanent sunlight.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"Energy storage usable specific energy","unit":"usable Watt-hours per kg of storage system","value":104.0,"range_low":70.0,"range_high":160.0,"notes":"v1.11.0.  130 Wh/kg at the system level (STORAGE_REFERENCE 'Li-ion battery (system level)': cells reach 250-300 Wh/kg and packaging, harness, balancing and thermal roughly halve it) × 0.80 depth of discharge = 104 Wh/kg USABLE.  NASA's Li-ion state of the art is 175 Wh/kg at 80% depth of discharge and 90% charge/discharge efficiency (Schmitz et al., IEEE Aerospace 2023, NTRS 20230001487, Table 3), so the 0.80 matches and the usable figure there is 140 Wh/kg; this row's 104 is 26% below it.  The 130 Wh/kg system figure has no source of its own.  Cells: ~265 Wh/kg (Ali et al., Frontiers in Energy Research, 2023).  DoD is folded in here rather than carried as a fourth row because a consumer that forgets to apply it silently oversizes the mission by 25%, and this table's job is to hand Module 4 the number it should divide by.\nA regenerative fuel cell (400 Wh/kg, TRL 5) is the obvious architecture for a multi-hour dark period and would cut this term by ~4×; it is not taken, because nothing has flown one and this row is the operational choice.  The ~4× is on storage mass only: NASA's 100 W demonstration measured 47.4% round trip (NASA/TM-20205000357, Table III), so at f = 0.50 the array oversize rises from 2.11× to 3.11× and part of the saving is paid back in array.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"Energy storage round-trip efficiency","unit":"fraction of stored energy recovered","value":0.9,"range_low":0.8,"range_high":0.95,"notes":"v1.11.0.  Charge and discharge losses through the cells and the regulator.  Li-ion cells alone run 0.92-0.96 round trip; 0.90 takes the loss through PMAD as well, and matches NASA's 90% charge/discharge efficiency for Li-ion (Schmitz et al. 2023, Table 3).  This is the term that makes the array oversize worse than the naive 1/(1−f): the energy that goes through the store has to be generated twice over, once for the load and once for the loss.  At f = 0.50 it is the difference between 2.00× and 2.11×.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"Power-system row baseline dark period","unit":"hours of darkness already covered by the 60 W/kg row","value":0.58,"range_low":0.0,"range_high":1.2,"notes":"v1.11.0.  The deduction that stops Module 4 double-charging the battery.  'Power system specific mass' is 60 W/kg SYSTEM-level against ROSA's ~150 W/kg at the wing, and part of that 2.5× is a battery — so some storage is already paid for and only the INCREMENT above it is new.\n0.58 h is the standard LEO eclipse (35 min of a ~92 min orbit), which is the storage duration a conventional deep-space PV train is specified against.  Arithmetic: 0.58 h of 1 W at 104 Wh/kg usable is 0.0056 kg/W, against the row's own 1/60 = 0.0167 kg/W of total plant — a third of it, which is why deducting it matters rather than being a nicety.\n⚠️  The 'Power system specific mass' row's own notes claim it covers 'power through eclipse and through the night side of a rotating body'.  It cannot cover both: an asteroid with a 10 h rotation is dark for 5 h, roughly 9× the LEO figure, and no single specific mass can be right for both duty cycles. That contradiction is the argon failure in a new place — a reference row asserting two incompatible states at once — and this row resolves it by naming which of the two the 60 W/kg figure actually is.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"Volatile cargo containment","unit":"kg of containment per kg of volatile cargo","value":0.05,"range_low":0.03,"range_high":0.12,"notes":"v1.11.0.  Water sold at a depot has to still be water when it arrives.  Exposed ice in sunlight at 1 AU sits far above its sublimation threshold and is simply gone over a multi-year cruise; shaded, sealed and blanketed it is stable for decades.  So the charge is a sealed shaded hold — no power, no cryocooler, but real mass.\nCarried in STORAGE_REFERENCE since v1.9.0 with '⚠️  NOT modelled in Module 4' on it, and duplicated here because that table is not one Module 4 loads.  It is INCREMENTAL to the 0.15 ore-restraint fraction Module 4 already flies as `return_structure_frac_of_payload`: the hopper holds the cargo, the seal and shade keep the volatile fraction of it from leaving.  That reading is what makes the storage row's own 'heavier than an ore hopper' true at a value below 0.15.\nCharged on WATER only.  (Until 0.12.4 this said 'which is what the citation covers', but the row cites nothing.)  ENGINEERING ESTIMATE: no published source gives the containment mass fraction, or the stability of a passive sealed, shaded water hold over a multi-year cruise.  NASA's long-term storage work (NASA/TM-2011-215988; Plachta et al. 2017) covers cryogenic propellant tanks with zero-boil-off hardware, not a passive water hold.  Carbon and organics are refractory at these temperatures and ride in the hopper like rock.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"Launch vehicle reliability","unit":"probability of a successful launch","value":0.97,"range_low":0.9,"range_high":0.99,"notes":"v1.7.0.  Falcon 9 has flown >99% success over 300+ flights. For a new vehicle, Cross & Vesely (NASA, NTRS 20180006947) built an assumed design from every failure on the first two flights of each vehicle model, 1980-2017: first-flight failure probability 0.134 (success 0.866), or 0.0898 (success 0.910) with heritage credit for three design elements.  The 0.90 low end is that heritage-credited case, not the raw new-vehicle rate.  0.97 is a fleet-representative figure for an operational booster on a high-value payload.  Distinct from launch insurance, which replaces the HARDWARE on failure — it does not replace the revenue the mission would have earned.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"Spacecraft mean time between failures","unit":"years of deep-space operation","value":30.0,"range_low":15.0,"range_high":60.0,"notes":"v1.7.0.  Exponential survival: P = exp(-T/MTBF).  Anchors span the record — Voyager 1/2 past 45 years, New Horizons 19+, Dawn 11 (ended on hydrazine exhaustion, not failure), against Akatsuki's orbit-insertion loss and Hayabusa's near-total systems failure at 4 years.  30 years puts a 5-year mission at 85% survival, which matches the broad deep-space record.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"Mining system first-of-kind success probability","unit":"probability the rig works as designed","value":0.85,"range_low":0.7,"range_high":0.95,"notes":"v1.8.1.  Probability the excavation and beneficiation chain works once it arrives — separate from the spacecraft surviving the trip.  Counted from the actual flight record of regolith-contact mechanisms rather than from the failures alone, which is what v1.7.0's 0.75 did and it was unfairly harsh:
  SUCCEEDED (10): Apollo 15-17 drills and scoops; Luna 16 / 20 / 24 drills; Stardust aerogel; Phoenix arm (sticky soil delayed delivery but it worked); Curiosity drill (feed mechanism failed 2016, recovered by feed-extended drilling); Hayabusa2 sampler and SCI impactor, both touchdowns clean; OSIRIS-REx TAGSAM, 121.6 g against a 60 g requirement; Perseverance coring drill; Chang'e 5 and 6 drill + scoop.  (The Curiosity entry is Kinnett, Green, Klein & Lin, JPL, Aerospace Mechanisms Symposium 2022: feed stall on sol 1536, first feed-extended sample on sol 2057.  Shapiro et al., Space Mechanisms Lessons Learned Study Vol. II, NASA TM-107047, 1995, sorts flight lessons by mechanism type.  The other entries are not yet cited.)
  PARTIAL (1): Hayabusa — the projectile never fired, but contact dust was still collected and returned.
  FAILED (2): Philae's harpoon pyrotechnics; InSight's HP3 mole, which could not get purchase in Martian regolith.
That is 11/13 = 0.85 counting Hayabusa as the success it ultimately was, or 10/13 = 0.77 counting it as a loss.  0.85 is taken because Hayabusa did return its sample.
The honest caveat is that NONE of these is sustained mining — they are one-shot or short-campaign collections of grams to kilograms, not a rig moving 200 kg/day for years with no maintenance.  0.85 is therefore the demonstrated mechanism rate, and the sustained-operation risk on top of it is carried by the spacecraft MTBF term rather than double-counted here.  Grows with flight heritage — see 'Mining reliability growth exponent'.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"Mining reliability growth exponent","unit":"Duane / AMSAA growth parameter (alpha)","value":0.3,"range_low":0.1,"range_high":0.6,"notes":"v1.9.0.  Reliability is not static across a programme — it grows as failure modes are found and designed out.  The Duane model has failure probability fall as n^(-alpha) with cumulative production (MIL-HDBK-189C, Jun 2011, 5.2.6).  The handbook's Table II gives historical growth rates of 0.27-0.64 for one-shot systems (median 0.47; the mean is printed '.046', evidently 0.46) and 0.23-0.53 for time-based ones (0.34 mean, 0.32 median), and rejects Duane's universal 0.5.  0.30 sits near the bottom of both ranges — appropriate for hardware that flies once every few years, where each mission is a slow, expensive lesson and there is no test fleet to accelerate the learning.  The 0.10 low end of the range is below every historical figure the handbook gives: a pessimistic sensitivity bound, not a sourced value.  Until 0.6.1 this note credited MIL-HDBK-189 with a 0.3-0.6 'active' and 0.1-0.2 'passive' band; the handbook draws no such split.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"Mining system mature success probability","unit":"asymptotic ceiling on rig success probability","value":0.95,"range_low":0.85,"range_high":0.99,"notes":"v1.9.0.  Growth is asymptotic, not unbounded — no amount of flight heritage makes a machine that grinds rock in vacuum certain to work.  0.95 is where mature, high-cycle spacecraft MECHANISMS sit.  The fleet record: of almost 400 satellites launched successfully 1958-1983, about 10% had some deployment anomaly, mostly mechanical (Shapiro et al., Space Mechanisms Lessons Learned Study Vol. I, NASA TM-107046, 1995).  That is a per-satellite anomaly rate, not a per-deployment success rate; the ~97-99% per deployment once given here is an estimate with no source.  A continuously-operating excavator is harder than a one-shot deployment.  Without this ceiling the Duane curve would eventually promise certainty, which no mechanism earns.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"Mining rig service life","unit":"years of operation before wear-out","value":15.0,"range_low":5.0,"range_high":30.0,"notes":"v1.7.0.  Caps how many missions one rig can actually serve, which the old flat amortisation ignored — you cannot spread a rig across 100 missions of 2 years each.  Bounded by abrasive wear on regolith-contact mechanisms, thermal cycling and radiation, not by propellant.  ISS-class hardware is rated 15-30 years; a machine chewing rock is at the low end.  Whatever life is left when the programme ends is credited back as terminal value.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"Mining rig maximum trips","unit":"mining campaigns before wear-out","value":5.0,"range_low":2.0,"range_high":12.0,"notes":"v1.12.0.  The SECOND half of rig service life, and the half that was missing: 'Mining rig service life' above is a CALENDAR bound, and calendar time is not what wears out a machine that cuts rock.  Duty cycles are.  A rig sitting idle between campaigns ages slowly; one digging continuously eats cutting surfaces, seals and bearings on unweathered, angular, never-water-rounded regolith.  Module 4 took min(years/stay) alone, so at a short stay one rig served 12 consecutive campaigns on the strength of a number that only ever said it would not corrode meanwhile.  ⚠️  JUDGEMENT, and there is no flight heritage for it — nothing has ever mined an asteroid twice.  Bracketed from the two nearest analogues, which disagree in the useful direction.  TERRESTRIAL: mobile mining plant reaches major overhaul near 15,000-25,000 operating hours (~2-3 yr of continuous duty, i.e. ~2 campaigns at this model's ~1.25 yr stay) and survives 2-3 rebuilds before the frame is retired — but every one of those rebuilds happens in a workshop, and there is no workshop at an asteroid.  FLIGHT: every regolith-contact mechanism ever flown was single-campaign by design or failed inside one — TAGSAM fired once, Philae's harpoons did not fire, InSight's mole never buried itself, and Curiosity's drill lost its feed mechanism partway through its first decade.  5 is therefore already the optimistic reading of both: rebuild-interval life, achieved un-rebuilt.  range_low 2 is one overhaul interval; range_high 12 restores the pre-v1.12.0 behaviour, where the calendar bound was the only bound.  Set Module 4's `model_rig_trip_limit = False` for that exactly.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"Rig salvage fraction","unit":"fraction of remaining book value recoverable","value":0.5,"range_low":0.0,"range_high":0.8,"notes":"v1.7.0.  A part-worn rig parked on a specific asteroid is worth something to whoever goes there next and nothing to anyone else — an illiquid, location-locked asset with a market of approximately one buyer.  Half of remaining book value is a deliberately unheroic haircut.  The one space-asset salvage estimate on record brackets it: NASA CR-3349 (1980) puts a solar power satellite's average salvage value at 5-10% of its capital cost, and a demonstration satellite's at 60-90% of its on-orbit cost.  Those are fractions of cost; this one is of remaining book value.  Set 0.0 to model abandonment.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"In-space processing plant throughput","unit":"kg processed per year per kg of plant","value":100.0,"range_low":20.0,"range_high":500.0,"notes":"v1.7.0.  Sizes the refinery that turns raw asteroid feedstock into something a depot can actually build with.  Terrestrial smelters run 1,000x their own mass per year (no source is given for this); 100x is a heavy derating for microgravity, no convection, no gravity-fed materials handling and full autonomy.  NASA's only published designs for in-space processing hardware run far lower: 7.28 kg per year per kg (a lunar water plant, Kleinhenz & Paz 2021, NTRS 20210016820) to 13.3 (a Mars propellant plant, Kleinhenz & Paz 2017, AIAA 2017-0423), the band of 'ISRU propellant plant throughput'.  This row's 100 is 7.5 to 14 times that, and its 20 floor is 1.5 times the top.  Nothing here shows why a mineral refinery should outrun ISRU hardware by that much; the value is an estimate.  Combined with the $300k/kg recurring hardware rate this sets the capital charge per kg refined.","reference_year":2026}

{"category":"ISRU propellant plant throughput","unit":"kg of propellant made per year per kg of plant","value":7.28,"range_low":7.28,"range_high":13.3,"notes":"Data contract 1.23.0.  Sizes the plant that electrolyses mined water and liquefies the products, for a propellant whose isru_processing_wh_per_kg is above zero (hydrolox).  Kleinhenz & Paz, 'A Lunar Water ISRU System Study for Human-Scale Propellant Production', PTMSS/SRR 2021 (NTRS 20210016820): the 'ridge' system (electrolyser, gas dryers, H2 and O2 liquefaction, storage tanks) is 2.6 t for 10 t of O2 and 1.67 t of H2 at MR 6 in 225 days, i.e. 11.67 t / 0.616 yr / 2.6 t = 7.28.  Its excavator and water extractor (the 0.49 t 'mine') are NOT in it; a consumer's rig and water-liberation energy already cover that half.  The value is an upper bound on mass, because the ridge includes the propellant tanks a return vehicle flies anyway; owner decision to take it over Johnson (AIAA ASCEND 2023)'s radiator-only floor of 3.9 kg/kW, which leaves out the electrolyser and the cryocoolers.  range_high 13.3: Kleinhenz & Paz, AIAA 2017-0423 (NTRS 20170005179), a whole Mars CH4/O2 system, 1.7 t for 29.7 t in 480 days.","reference_year":2026}

def typed(x):

    return [t,repr(x)]


def digest(x):
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(typed(x),ensure_ascii=False,separators=(',',':')).encode()).hexdigest()


ORIGINAL_LADDER=calc._programme_ladder_cached
ORIGINAL_WINDOW=calc._delivery_window_yr


def run(f,diagnostic):
    fleet=f['fleet'];waves=f.get('waves',1);n=fleet*waves
    name=f.get('mineral','magnetite')
    row=dict(designation='R352 '+f['id'],name=f['id'],diameter_km=1.,density_gcm3=3.,
        estimated_mass_kg=3e12*math.pi/6,semi_major_axis_au=f.get('a',1.2),eccentricity=0.,
        inclination_deg=0.,rotation_period_h=10.,comp_ice_fraction=0.,comp_carbon_fraction=0.,
        comp_metal_fraction=(1. if name=='nickel-iron' else 0.),
        comp_silicate_fraction=(0. if name=='nickel-iron' else 1.),
        comp_pgm_enrichment=1.,comp_phases=json.dumps({name:1.}))
    cfg=calc.CalcConfig(delivery_destination='cislunar',use_beneficiation=False,
        market_model=f.get('market','capacity_cap'),optimise_programme_scale=True,
        model_refinery=False,model_launch_windows=False,use_isru_return_propellant=False,
        model_reliability=False,max_fleet_ships=fleet,nre_amortization_missions=1,
        apply_wacc_compounding=False,sell_surplus_at_discount=f.get('surplus',True),
        surplus_price_fraction=f.get('surplus_fraction',.5))
    m=mineral.copy(deep=True);m.attrs={}
    o=ops.copy(deep=True);o.attrs={}
    v=copy.deepcopy(vehicles.loc[vehicles['name']==f.get('vehicle','Falcon 9 (reusable)')].iloc[0].to_dict())
    p=copy.deepcopy(props.loc[props['name']=='kerolox  (RP-1 / LOX)'].iloc[0].to_dict())
    ladder_events=[];window_events=[]

    def restrict_ladder(rig_trips,config,market_mode=None):
        choices,original_fleet=ORIGINAL_LADDER(rig_trips,config,market_mode)
        chosen=(n,fleet,waves)
        assert chosen in choices,(f['id'],chosen,rig_trips,choices)
        ladder_events.append(dict(chosen=chosen,original_choices=len(choices),
            original_contains_chosen=True,rig_trips=rig_trips))
        return [chosen],[fleet]

    def calendar_window(count,ships,duration,cadence):
        assert (count,ships)==(n,fleet)
        native=ORIGINAL_WINDOW(count,ships,duration,cadence)
        # The cost calendar explicitly says wave w sells at T+w*cadence.
        # One repeated rectangular fleet therefore ends at T+(W-1)*cadence.
        span=duration+(waves-1)*cadence
        cohort_window=span/count
        used=cohort_window if diagnostic and fleet>1 else native
        assert math.isclose(count*native-span,cadence*(1-1/fleet),rel_tol=1e-10,abs_tol=1e-12)
        window_events.append(dict(n=count,fleet=ships,waves=waves,duration=duration,cadence=cadence,
            native_per_delivery_window=native,cohort_per_delivery_window=cohort_window,
            used_window=used,reported_span=span,native_accumulation_horizon=count*native,
            excess_horizon=count*native-span))
        return used

    calc._programme_ladder_cached=restrict_ladder
    calc._delivery_window_yr=calendar_window
    try:
        result=calc.evaluate_asteroid(row,{'minerals':m,'ops':o},cfg,combos=[(v,p)])
    finally:
        calc._programme_ladder_cached=ORIGINAL_LADDER
        calc._delivery_window_yr=ORIGINAL_WINDOW
    assert result is not None,f['id']
    assert result['programme_missions']==n
    assert result['m_launch_kg']<=v['payload_leo_kg']*(1+1e-8)
    assert result['feed_processed_kg']<=result['throughput_cap_kg']*(1+1e-9)
    assert n*(result['feed_processed_kg']+result['isru_feed_kg'])<=row['estimated_mass_kg']*(1+1e-9)
    assert result['mission_duration_yr']<=cfg.max_mission_duration_yr*(1+1e-9)
    assert result['mining_duration_yr']<=cfg.max_mining_duration_yr*(1+1e-9)
    assert result['return_volume_m3']<=.25*v['fairing_volume_m3']*(1+1e-9)
    assert math.isclose(result['programme_span_yr'],result['mission_duration_yr']+
        (waves-1)*result['campaign_cadence_yr'],rel_tol=1e-12)
    # This observer is valid for these single-market, raw, one-phase fixtures.
    phase=calc.asteroid_phase_table(row,m)
    assert len(phase)==1 and phase[0][0]==name and phase[0][1]==1.
    markets=calc.market_table(m)
    cap=calc.phase_market_kg(markets,name)
    payload=result['max_payload_kg']
    if cfg.market_model=='capacity_cap':
        assert window_events
        event=window_events[0]
        # All candidate ratios share the raw-payload architecture in this audit.
        sold_full=payload-result['surplus_payload_kg']-result['unsold_payload_kg']
        adopted_frac=cfg.surplus_price_fraction if cfg.sell_surplus_at_discount else 0.
        gross_oracle=(min(payload,cap*event['used_window'])+
            max(0.,payload-cap*event['used_window'])*adopted_frac)*phase[0][2]
        assert math.isclose(result['gross_value_usd'],gross_oracle,rel_tol=2e-12),(f['id'],gross_oracle,result['gross_value_usd'])
        observer=dict(payload_kg=payload,price_usd_per_kg=phase[0][2],annual_cap_kg=cap,
            full_price_kg_per_mission=sold_full,programme_full_price_kg=n*sold_full,
            programme_budget_kg=cap*result['programme_span_yr'],
            budget_excess_kg=n*sold_full-cap*result['programme_span_yr'],
            window=event)
        with localcontext() as ctx:
            ctx.prec=50
            t=Decimal(str(result['mission_duration_yr']))
            cadence=Decimal(str(result['campaign_cadence_yr']))
            rate=Decimal(str(cap))
            # Enumerate sales by wave, independently of either window helper.
            sales=[dict(time_yr=str(t+w*cadence),deliveries=fleet) for w in range(waves)]
            end=max(Decimal(x['time_yr']) for x in sales)
            source_horizon=t+Decimal(n-1)*cadence/Decimal(fleet)
            excess=source_horizon-end
            assert excess==cadence*(1-Decimal(1)/Decimal(fleet))
            assert math.isclose(float(end),result['programme_span_yr'],rel_tol=1e-14)
            assert math.isclose(float(excess),event['excess_horizon'],rel_tol=1e-10,abs_tol=1e-12)
            observer['independent_50_digit_clock']=dict(sales=sales,end_yr=str(end),
                accumulation_budget_kg=str(rate*end),source_accumulation_horizon_yr=str(source_horizon),
                extra_horizon_yr=str(excess),extra_full_price_budget_kg=str(rate*excess))
    else:
        assert not window_events
        observer=dict(payload_kg=payload,price_usd_per_kg=phase[0][2],annual_cap_kg=cap,
            out_of_scope_market=cfg.market_model)
    return result,row,ladder_events,window_events,observer,v,p
